About

I teach English to classes of 15–30 adult and young-adult students, and it's that classroom, watching what actually lands with a learner versus what just sounds good in a lesson plan, that pulled me toward instructional design. A course only works if someone gets through it and remembers something afterward; everything else is decoration.

My Master's research looked at how teachers' formative feedback affects learners' spoken performance in EFL classrooms, which is really a question about how adults learn from feedback loops, not just language. That question shows up again in every module I build: where does a learner need a nudge, a check, a chance to get something wrong safely before it matters.

The four modules in this portfolio are self-directed projects, built to demonstrate range across adult learning contexts: a soft-skills topic, a compliance topic, a technical safety topic, and a new-hire onboarding topic, rather than commissioned client work. I'm currently looking for the first real one.

Module 01: Language & communication

Business English Essentials: Professional Emails and Meetings

Level B1–B2 Format Self-paced, 15–20 min Audience Adult learners: ESL / EFL / EAL professionals

A short-form module built for learners who already have working English but freeze up in professional situations: writing a clear email, sounding appropriately direct (not rude) in a meeting, following the unwritten conventions of workplace correspondence.

Rather than teaching grammar in isolation, the module works through realistic email and meeting scenarios, asking learners to choose or produce the more appropriate phrasing and explaining why one option lands better than another in a professional register.

Module 02: Compliance & awareness

Cybersecurity Essentials: Protecting the Workplace from Everyday Threats

Format Self-paced Audience General workforce, no technical background assumed

Security-awareness training lives or dies on whether it feels relevant to someone who isn't in IT. This module keeps the focus on the everyday moments where a breach actually starts: a convincing phishing email, a weak shared password, an unlocked screen, rather than abstract policy language.

Each section pairs a realistic threat scenario with a short decision point, so the learner practices spotting the warning sign in context instead of just reading a list of rules.

Module 03: Technical & safety

Aviation Ground Safety: FOD Prevention and Ramp Operations Essentials

Format Self-paced Audience Ground crew / ramp operations staff

Foreign Object Debris (FOD) is one of those risks that's completely preventable and still causes real damage every year, because it comes down to habits, not knowledge gaps. This module was designed around that gap, walking through what counts as FOD, where it collects on a ramp, and the daily habits that keep it out of the way.

The module leans on visual, spatial content: ramp layouts, equipment identification, since ground safety training has to translate into what someone actually does with their hands and eyes on shift, not just what they can recite.

Module 04: Onboarding

Insurance Fundamentals for New Agents: Policies, Terms, and Claims Essentials

Format Self-paced Audience Newly hired insurance agents

New agents are handed a wall of policy terminology in week one and expected to sound confident on a client call by week two. This module breaks that wall down into the vocabulary and concepts a new hire actually needs first: policy structure, common terms, and how a claim moves from filed to resolved.

It's built as an onboarding piece rather than a reference manual: sequenced so each concept sets up the next one, with checks along the way to confirm the terminology has actually landed before moving on.
